<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Systematic evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is crucial for advancing Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). However, existing benchmarks remain insufficient for rigorously assessing their constrained reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MapTab</span>, a multimodal benchmark specifically designed to evaluate constrained reasoning in MLLMs via route planning tasks. MapTab requires MLLMs to perceive and ground visual cues from map images alongside route attributes (e.g., Time, Price) from structured tabular data. The benchmark encompasses two scenarios: <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metromap</span>, covering metro networks in <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">160</span> cities across <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">52</span> countries, and <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Travelmap</span>, depicting <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">168</span> representative tourist attractions from <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">19</span> countries. In total, MapTab comprises <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">328</span> images, <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">196,800</span> route planning queries, and 3,936 QA queries, all incorporating 4 key constraints: Time, Price, Comfort, and Reliability. Extensive evaluations across 15 representative MLLMs reveal that current models face substantial challenges in constrained multimodal reasoning. Notably, under conditions of limited visual perception, multimodal collaboration often underperforms compared to unimodal approaches. We believe MapTab provides a challenging and realistic testbed to advance the systematic evaluation of MLLMs. Our code is available at <a href="https://github.com/Ziqiao-Shang/MapTab" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Ziqiao-Shang/MapTab</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">

</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>

</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> integrate cross-modal representations and techniques such as visual chain-of-thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and multi-dimensional perception <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, enabling remarkable reasoning capabilities and applications in complex decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, game agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, and autonomous driving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Accordingly, systematic evaluation of MLLMs has become a critical yet challenging research direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Early benchmarks, including MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and V*-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie, 2024</a>)</cite> <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span>, focused on basic and structured visual reasoning, while maps naturally integrating topology and semantics, have been increasingly adopted to evaluate MLLMs in multi-scale geographic and complex topological reasoning, as reflected in benchmarks such as Mapbench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xing et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, ReasonMap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>, and RewardMap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these advances, existing benchmarks remain insufficient to characterize constrained multimodal reasoning. Such reasoning requires models to simultaneously satisfy multiple constraints, temporal, spatial, and resource based, within a unified framework to support robust and personalized decision-making. Map-based multimodal route planning (RP) offers a representative evaluation setting, as maps provide explicit structured information that enables systematic assessment of long-tracing reasoning. RP is inherently multi-factor and strongly constrained, demanding the joint optimization of efficiency, cost, comfort, and reliability across diverse user preferences. These trade-offs, which vary systematically across user groups, closely mirror real-world industrial route planning systems and place substantial demands on models’ holistic reasoning and constraint-handling capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by these observations, we propose MapTab, a multimodal evaluation framework based on <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">vision-structured data</em> collaborative modeling for heterogeneous topological reasoning under complex constraints. As shown in Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>, MapTab covers two scenarios, Metromap and Travelmap, comprising a total of <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">328</span> images, where Metromap includes metro maps from <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">52</span> countries and <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">160</span> cities worldwide, and Travelmap consists of travel maps from <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">19</span> countries depicting <span id="S1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">168</span> representative tourist attractions. Since a single map image cannot incorporate essential quantitative attributes such as time, price, <span id="S1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span>, which are crucial for constraint-based decision-making, we introduce two complementary tables, Vertex_tab and Edge_tab, to store these attributes in a structured format. Moreover, representing the map as a graph structure allows for a clear depiction of both the attributes of stations/attractions and the relationships between them, aligning with the topological nature of the problem. For the core RP task, MapTab includes <span id="S1.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16,400</span> origin-destination pairs, yielding <span id="S1.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">196,800</span> unconstrained and multi-constrained RP queries. Furthermore, MapTab offers 3,936 QA queries, which are designed to support a comprehensive analysis of the benchmark characteristics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">MapTab introduces substantial improvements over existing benchmarks and fills several critical gaps in current evaluation frameworks: 1) <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-constraint evaluation:</span> To address the lack of benchmarks incorporating realistic constraints, MapTab integrates multiple constraints into RP tasks, enabling MLLMs to generate personalized and robust decisions. 2) <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Topology-focused reasoning:</span> To overcome distractions from redundant visual details in traditional maps, MapTab uses metro and scenic-area topology maps with time, cost, comfort, and reliability encoded in a heterogeneous graph, reducing perceptual complexity and isolating reasoning performance. 3) <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision-structured data collaboration:</span> To overcome the reliance on image and unstructured text modalities in existing datasets, MapTab combines map images with tabular node attributes to assess joint visual-structured reasoning, ranging from complementary reasoning between maps and node attributes when edge-based topology is not provided, to selective exploitation of topological information from multiple modalities when edge_tab are available.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, our contributions are threefold:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal multi-constraint benchmark:</span> MapTab first combines visual and structured data in route planning tasks to assess MLLMs’ reasoning over heterogeneous, multi-constraint graphs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Large-scale dual-scenario benchmark:</span> MapTab comprises a total of <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">328</span> maps, with Metromap images spanning <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">52</span> countries and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">160</span> cities, and Travelmap images covering <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">19</span> countries and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">168</span> tourist attractions. It also includes <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16,400</span> origin-destination pairs, <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">196,800</span> RP queries, and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3,936</span> QA queries, offering a comprehensive benchmark for analysis.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comprehensive MLLM evaluation:</span> We assess 15 long-context MLLMs on constraints, multimodal collaboration, and reasoning chains, revealing performance limits under multi-constraint settings.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Task Definition</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given an image <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>, an edge information table (Edge_tab <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>), a node information table (Vertex_tab <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>), and a route planning query <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, the objective of MLLMs is to generate an optimal planned route <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> based on these inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, the <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">input</span> <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(I,E,V,Q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(I,E,V,Q)</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as follows: <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the input metro map (or scenic route map); <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E=(\hat{T}_{e},\hat{P}_{e},\hat{C}_{e},\hat{R}_{e})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E=(\hat{T}_{e},\hat{P}_{e},\hat{C}_{e},\hat{R}_{e})</annotation></semantics></math> represents Edge_tab, which records the normalized time <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{T}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{T}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, price <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, comfort level <math id="S2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{C}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{C}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, and reliability <math id="S2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{R}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{R}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> for each metro line (or inter-attraction commuting path) in the image; <math id="S2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V=(\hat{T}_{v},\hat{P}_{v},\hat{C}_{v},\hat{R}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V=(\hat{T}_{v},\hat{P}_{v},\hat{C}_{v},\hat{R}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math> represents Vertex_tab, which stores the same multi-dimensional attributes for each metro station (or scenic spot); the text query Q is a multi-constraint query that includes starting point <math id="S2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, destination point <math id="S2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and user’s constraints, where <math id="S2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> both corresponding to metro stations (or scenic spots) in the image.
The <span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">output</span> is an optimal planned route <math id="S2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, represented as an ordered sequence of nodes starting from <math id="S2.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and ending at <math id="S2.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id="S2.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{*}=(v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{*}=(v_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{k})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{1}=s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{1}=s</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{k}=t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{k}=t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimization Objective</span>: Given a starting station/spot <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and a target station/spot <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the objective is to find the optimal route <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> that minimizes the overall path cost:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r^{*}=\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}(s,t)}\Big[w_{1}T(r,\hat{T}_{e},\hat{T}_{v})+w_{2}P(r,\hat{P}_{e},\hat{P}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>arg</mi><mi>min</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r^{*}=\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}(s,t)}\Big[w_{1}T(r,\hat{T}_{e},\hat{T}_{v})+w_{2}P(r,\hat{P}_{e},\hat{P}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(s,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}(s,t)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of all feasible routes from <math id="S2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(r,\hat{T}_{e},\hat{T}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(r,\hat{T}_{e},\hat{T}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(r,\hat{P}_{e},\hat{P}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(r,\hat{P}_{e},\hat{P}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-C(r,\hat{C}_{e},\hat{C}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-C(r,\hat{C}_{e},\hat{C}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-R(r,\hat{R}_{e},\hat{R}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-R(r,\hat{R}_{e},\hat{R}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the Time, Price, Comfort Level, and Reliability costs of route <math id="S2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. The weights <math id="S2.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> balance the path cost factors to minimize the overall cost.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:300.2pt;"><img src="2602.18600v1/Figures/fig_2.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:414/229;" width="414" height="229" alt="Refer to caption">
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.fig1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Schematic overview of the MapTab construction pipeline, comprising 5 main steps: Image Collection &amp; Preprocessing, Tabular Construction, Quality Control, Query Generation, and Label Annotation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>MapTab Building Pipeline</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study introduces MapTab, a multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs on multi-constraint heterogeneous graph reasoning across two scenarios, Metromap and Travelmap (see Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Benchmark Statistics ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>). As shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F2.fig1" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 Task Definition ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we curate 328 high-quality maps (see Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Metromap/Travelmap Image Collection and Preprocessing ‣ 3.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>) and use structured tables to store multi-dimensional node and edge attributes (see Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Constraint Condition Tabular Construction ‣ 3.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>), with a dual-track quality control process ensuring the reliability of the benchmark and its annotations (see Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS3" title="3.2.3 Quality Control ‣ 3.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.3</span></a>). Using deterministic algorithms, we generate a complete set of queries for RP tasks and QA tasks, evaluating MLLM reasoning robustness with varied instruction templates (see Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Queries Construction ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Benchmark Statistics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MapTab comprises two scenarios, Metromap and Travelmap, both represented in the form of topological graphs. Metromap includes 160 maps covering 52 countries, involving 32 native languages, with images rendered in 28 languages and an average resolution of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4{,}140\times 3{,}744" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4,140</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3,744</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4{,}140\times 3{,}744</annotation></semantics></math> pixels. Travelmap consists of 168 maps covering 19 countries, involving 15 native languages, with images rendered in 5 languages and an average resolution of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{,}126\times 1{,}352" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1,126</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1,352</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}126\times 1{,}352</annotation></semantics></math> pixels, containing relatively less information than Metromap. Maps in both scenarios are categorized into three difficulty levels, easy, medium, and hard, with a strictly balanced ratio of 1:1:1 across difficulty levels. The image split between the training and test sets follows a 2:1 ratio (218 images for training and 110 images for testing).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MapTab defines a total of 16,400 base origin-destination pairs (8,000 for Metromap and 8,400 for Travelmap), which are split into training and test sets at a ratio of 4:1 (13,120 for training and 3,280 for testing). As a result, the average number of origin-destination pairs per training image is approximately twice that of the test images. Queries are generated based on these origin-destination pairs and include three types of unconstrained queries and nine types of multi-constrained queries, yielding a total of 196,800 evaluation queries. These queries are evenly distributed across the three difficulty levels (easy, medium, and hard) with a 1:1:1 ratio. In addition, MapTab contains 3,936 QA queries, with 12 questions per image. QA queries are not split into training and test sets and are not assigned difficulty levels. Instead, all images are treated as test data and are used solely for MLLM evaluation and benchmark characteristic analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Data Collection and Preprocessing</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Metromap/Travelmap Image Collection and Preprocessing</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure data quality, we collect map images with clear backgrounds and high resolution from multiple public online sources whenever possible. During preprocessing, we discard maps with cluttered backgrounds, incorrect annotations, handwritten content, or overly personalized designs, and regenerate or manually correct them as needed. For Travelmap, in cases where direct routes exist between distant attractions but are not explicitly connected, we randomly add loop connections to enhance the completeness of the topological structure. All images are publicly sourced and properly licensed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Constraint Condition Tabular Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to the “image + unstructured text" paradigm, the “image + table" paradigm provides a strong structural prior. In RP tasks, tables encode node and edge attributes in a low-entropy, high signal-to-noise manner, effectively avoiding the semantic ambiguity and redundancy inherent in natural language descriptions. Specifically, by combining Gemini-3-Flash, validation algorithms, and manual correction (see Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS3" title="3.2.3 Quality Control ‣ 3.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing ‣ 3 MapTab Building Pipeline ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.3</span></a>), we generate <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Edge_tab</span> and <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vertex_tab</span>, enabling multi-constraint information to be modeled in the form of heterogeneous graphs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Metromap is designed to simulate real-world urban commuting scenarios. Its <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Edge_tab</span> includes six key attributes: Edge, Line, Time, Price, Comfort Level, and Reliability. The Edge column follows the topological annotation format of FarPlanning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, while the numerical design of the remaining attributes is informed by metro operational characteristics and user experience (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1.SSS1" title="E.1.1 Metromap-Edge_tab ‣ E.1 Prompts for Generating Edge_tab and Vertex_tab ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.1</span></a>). On this basis, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vertex_tab</span> introduces an additional Transfer Time dimension to supplement the time cost not covered by the Time column during transfers (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1.SSS2" title="E.1.2 Metromap-Vertex_tab ‣ E.1 Prompts for Generating Edge_tab and Vertex_tab ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.2</span></a>). In contrast, Travelmap focuses on semantic evaluation and user psychological modeling. Compared with Metromap, it removes the Line and Transfer Time dimensions, retaining only five columns, Edge, Time, Price, Comfort Level, and Reliability, in both Edge_tab and Vertex_tab. The numerical values in Travelmap are primarily designed with reference to rating systems in real-world travel applications and map-provided indicative information (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1.SSS3" title="E.1.3 Travelmap-Edge_tab ‣ E.1 Prompts for Generating Edge_tab and Vertex_tab ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.3</span></a> and <a href="#A5.SS1.SSS4" title="E.1.4 Travelmap-Vertex_tab ‣ E.1 Prompts for Generating Edge_tab and Vertex_tab ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.4</span></a>). MapTab provides data in both CSV and JSON formats to explore the impact of tabular formats on experimental outcomes (see Appendix <a href="#A6.SS5" title="F.5 Ablation study of Tabular Modality ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3 </span>Quality Control</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the accuracy of Edge_tab and Vertex_tab, we implement dedicated validation algorithms for Metromap and Travelmap (see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Quality Control: Metromap Validation Algorithm ‣ Appendix B More Details for Dataset Construction ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> and <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Quality Control: Travelmap Validation Algorithm ‣ Appendix B More Details for Dataset Construction ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>) to pre-verify outputs from Gemini-3-Flash. Each result is then manually checked, ensuring reliability across the entire data pipeline.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Queries Construction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our queries consist of RP queries and QA queries, which together constitute essential inputs to the model. RP queries are designed to assess its ability to handle constraint-based reasoning and optimization tasks. On the other hand, QA queries evaluate model performance in answering diverse questions based on maps. RP queries comprise 12 distinct categories, including 3 unconstrained and 9 constraint-aware variants (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 RP Query ‣ Appendix D Query Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>), whereas QA queries span a total of 24 categories (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 QA Query ‣ Appendix D Query Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>). The construction of RP queries and QA queries is based on the previously generated Edge_tab and Vertex_tab, and is fully automated using deterministic Python programs. Under the assumption that Edge_tab and Vertex_tab themselves contain no structural or semantic errors, the generated queries exhibit verifiable completeness in terms of logical consistency and formal correctness, and are theoretically free from additional construction-induced bias or noise. This section focuses on the RP query construction process, and details of QA query construction are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 RP Query Distribution Based on Difficulty Classification Metrics ‣ Appendix B More Details for Dataset Construction ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>Question Generation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We divide RP tasks into <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">unconstrained</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">constrained</span> categories, using a unified route generation logic for both Metromap and Travelmap. For unconstrained tasks, we evaluate models’ parsing capabilities using three input modalities: <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Map only</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edge_tab only</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Map + Edge_tab</span>, where Edge_tab contains only <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edge Column</span> without constraints. To reduce semantic bias, each modality is paired with five distinct instruction templates (Direct Optimization, Graph-theoretic, Instruction-seeking, User-oriented, and Constraint-explicit; see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 RP Query ‣ Appendix D Query Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>), applied cyclically across questions and origin-destination pairs. Origin-destination pairs are sampled from the topological graph of Edge_tab (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 RP Query Distribution Based on Difficulty Classification Metrics ‣ Appendix B More Details for Dataset Construction ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>) and shortest paths are computed with <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dijkstra</span> algorithm until quotas are met. Each route contains at least three stations to guarantee meaningful tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For constrained tasks, we define nine scenarios, including four single-constraint settings (Time, Price, Comfort Level, Reliability) and five multi-constraint combinations. For multi-constraint tasks with Map + Edge_tab + Vertex_tab, MapTab simulates diverse user preferences: younger users prioritize time efficiency and cost (Time + Price + Reliability), middle-aged users balance efficiency and comfort (Time + Comfort Level + Reliability), older users emphasize affordability and travel comfort (Price + Comfort Level + Reliability), and families consider all four factors. With Map + Vertex2_tab, where Vertex2_tab integrates partial Edge_tab information to reduce reliance on topological cues (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Prompts for RP Queries ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>), only the full combination of all four factors is used. During evaluation, only relevant columns are given to the model to reduce context length.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Reference Route Collection and Label Annotation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The generation of reference routes follows a similar strategy to origin-destination sampling. First, the graph topology is derived from Edge_tab, and all shortest paths are computed using <span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dijkstra</span> algorithm. For constrained scenarios, the key difference from unconstrained scenarios lies in the preprocessing of per-dimension weights, which are normalized to a unified scale and combined via weighted aggregation to compute route scores (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Prompts for RP Queries ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>). For transfer stations, a “(transfer)” marker is appended to the station name, resulting in route representations such as “A-B(transfer)-C”. Finally, four aggregate metrics, Total_Time, Total_Price, Average_Comfort Level, and Average_Reliability, are appended to each route label to support ablation studies on constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setups</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents a systematic evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art long-context VLM on MapTab, comparing the performance of open-source and closed-source models on RP tasks across two scenarios. Experimental details for QA tasks are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluated Models.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We systematically evaluate multiple categories of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which are divided according to their reasoning mechanisms into general instruction-following models and reasoning-enhanced models with long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT) capabilities. The former category includes the Qwen3-VL-Instruct series (2B, 8B, 30B-A3B, 32B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, Phi-3.5-Vision-Instruct (4B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct (6B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, InternVL3-Instruct (8B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GPT-4.1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025a</a>)</cite>, and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2025</a>)</cite>. The latter category includes Qwen3-VL-Thinking (8B, 32B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, Doubao-Seed-1-6-251015-Thinking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">ByteDance Seed Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3-VL-Plus-Thinking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. To ensure fairness and reproducibility, we adopt unified protocols for model selection, deployment, parameter configuration, and multimodal input preprocessing. Detailed settings are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Experimental Settings ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For model performance evaluation, RP tasks are assessed using three metrics:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Exact Match Accuracy (EMA):</span> EMA evaluates whether the generated route exactly matches the reference path in station order and content, allowing minor spelling variations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Partial Match Accuracy (PMA):</span> PMA measures the proportion of the longest contiguous correct prefix from the origin, reflecting partial path consistency.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Difficulty-aware Score (DS):</span> DS incorporates task difficulty by weighting exact matches according to the combined Map_Difficulty and Query_Difficulty levels, thereby characterizing model robustness on harder instances.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Detailed definitions of these metrics are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Performance Metrics ‣ Appendix C Metrics ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>. In addition, we design multiple indicators to characterize Map_Difficulty and Query_Difficulty. Further details are given in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Difficulty Classification Metrics ‣ Appendix C Metrics ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Experimental Results</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> systematically reveals the reasoning capabilities and performance limitations of MLLMs on constrained heterogeneous graph tasks from four perspectives: modality comparison, constraint effects, multimodal collaboration, and explicit reasoning chains.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 1: Visual perception bottlenecks lead to over-reliance on structured data.</span> Across models, Map-only inputs consistently yield lower performance than Edge_tab-only inputs, reflecting the difficulty of recovering accurate topology from pixel-level map images, especially in the presence of crossings or overlapping structures. Morover, in dense or low-resolution settings, even basic optical character recognition (OCR) and entity identification become unreliable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 2: Constraints exert a dual effect on model reasoning.</span> Introducing constraints generally increases reasoning burden and degrades performance. However, we observe a counterintuitive anchoring effect: in visually dense MetroMap scenarios, Map + Vertex2_tab substantially outperforms the Map-only setting. This improvement likely arises because Vertex2_tab provides reliable symbolic anchors that correct OCR and entity recognition errors, with the benefits of accurate entity grounding outweighing the added reasoning cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 3: Multiple effects of multimodal interaction.</span> To investigate the synergy between visual and structured data, we compare Edge_tab-only versus Map + Edge_tab across Metromap and Travelmap scenarios. For Instruct models, in the visually dense Metromap tasks, Map + Edge_tab underperforms Edge_tab alone due to interference from complex visuals that disrupt text-based CoT reasoning. However, in simpler Travelmap scenarios, multimodal inputs generally enhance performance, highlighting the limited robustness of cross-modal integration under high visual complexity. For Thinking models, all Qwen-series Thinking models show notable improvements, reflecting effective synergy between text and visual inputs through CoT, whereas the Doubao model performs similarly across modalities, indicating that it reaches information saturation with text alone, and CoT does not further extend its reasoning capability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 4: Explicit reasoning chains exhibit a double-edged effect.</span> Explicit reasoning chains generally enhance performance for complex, compositional tasks. However, in simpler constrained Travelmap scenarios, Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking slightly underperforms its Instruct variant. This observation further supports the hypothesis that chain-of-thought prompting cannot surpass a model’s intrinsic upper bound of reasoning capability.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.2 </span>Ablation Study for Constraints</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Tables <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we conduct ablation studies on RP tasks to evaluate the impact of constraints on path selection.
In Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and fixing both the start and end stations, the changes between constrained paths and shortest paths can be categorized into three types after introducing constraints: 1) <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fully Repeat (FR)</span>: The shortest path is unique, and the constrained path remains unchanged. 2) <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Partially Repeat (PR)</span>: Multiple shortest paths exist, and the constrained path matches one of them. 3) <span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Not Repeat (NR)</span>: The shortest path is unique, but the constrained path differs. When multiple shortest paths exist, no misaligned paths are observed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, to examine the models’ understanding and computational ability regarding constraints, we require both Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and GPT-4o to output the constraint-related indicators, Total Time (T), Total Price (P), Average Comfort Level (C), and Average Reliability (R), for the optimal path in each task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the results from the following four aspects:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 1: “Shortest-path trap".</span> As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, high performance is concentrated in the FR category. In the Metromap scenario, when the numbers of PR and NR samples are 957 and 2481 respectively, their effective planning ratios are only 0.73% and 2.74%. This suggests that models primarily depend on shortest-path guessing, succeeding only when the shortest path happens to meet the constraints, rather than truly understanding them.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 2: Counting and numerical computation deficiencies.</span> Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that models struggle with numerical tasks like counting and computation. When asked to provide computed values, performance declines. QA experiments in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a> show that, while the models exhibit cross-modal integration capabilities, they struggle with tasks such as station counting, numerical comparison, and multi-hop reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 3: Heterogeneous graphs limited understanding.</span> Results from Tables <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> both show that model performance drops to near 0 on weighted and heterogeneous graph tasks, with little improvement even under simplified constraints. This indicates that current models have difficulties in modeling weight relations, which are further amplified in heterogeneous graph settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation 4: Multi-step Reasoning Bottleneck.</span> As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, all time-related indicators drop to zero once “transfer time” is introduced, revealing that models fail under even minimal multi-step reasoning complexity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.3 </span>Ablation Study of RP for Resolution</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To analyze the effects of visual perception degradation across 2 task types, Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates the impact of different image resolutions on RP task under two scenarios:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metromap scenario.</span> Under Map+Edge_tab and Map+E_tab+V_tab, image downsampling improves performance despite reduced visual fidelity, indicating that models primarily rely on E_tab while visual maps may introduce interference. Under Map+V_tab, performance remains largely stable, suggesting dependence on global graph information rather than local visual details. In contrast, in the Map-only setting, performance consistently degrades with downsampling, demonstrating that purely visual reasoning is highly sensitive to visual quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Travelmap scenario.</span> Downsampling generally degrades performance, but a rebound under the E_tab setting indicates that models initially attend to both visual and tabular inputs, but progressively shift their reasoning toward E_tab as image quality degrades. These results suggest that E_tab parsing defines the performance floor, whereas visual perception quality determines the performance ceiling. Thus, improving model’s performance ceiling is more fundamentally contingent upon the accurate perception and stable representation of crucial information in complex images.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.4 </span>Other Experimental Results</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following summarizes the five groups of experimental results presented in the Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">QA task performance evaluation</span> <span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>):</span> Models perform well on localization tasks, but struggle with counting, numerical computation, and multi-step reasoning tasks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Analysis across different Map Difficulty and Query Difficulty levels</span> <span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Ablation study of Map difficulty and Query difficulty ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>):</span> Performance degradation patterns differ significantly as Map and Query Difficulty levels increase, particularly between Metromap and Travelmap.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Impact of image resolution on QA tasks</span> <span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS4" title="F.4 Ablation study of QA for resolution ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.4</span></a>):</span> Improvements in image clarity alone do not constitute a sufficient condition for enhancing model performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Impact of tabular modality formats on RP and QA tasks</span> <span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS5" title="F.5 Ablation study of Tabular Modality ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.5</span></a>):</span> CSV format significantly reduces token overhead without inducing noticeable performance degradation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Impact of language distribution on RP tasks</span> <span id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS6" title="F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.6</span></a>):</span> Models perform better when the image language is high-frequency languages (e.g., Chinese or English), while differences in native language have a relatively limited impact on performance.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study introduces <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MapTab</span>, a multimodal benchmark for multi-constraint heterogeneous graph reasoning that jointly leverages <em id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">images and structured data</em>. Covering two real-world scenarios, <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Metromap</span> and <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Travelmap</span>, MapTab provides 328 de-redundant maps with multi-dimensional constraints in <span id="S5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edge_tab</span> and <span id="S5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex_tab</span>, generating 196,800 RP samples and 3,936 QA samples for comprehensive evaluation. Systematic testing of 15 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals enduring challenges in dense visual perception, multimodal integration, constraint reasoning, and long-horizon numerical or multi-step tasks. As MapTab currently targets static topological graphs, these findings emphasize the importance of exploring dynamic environments, more complex maps, and real-time reasoning in the future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine
Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none
which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>
