<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Reasoning Abilities in LLMs and MLLMs</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rapid rise of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2023</a>)</cite> has fundamentally reshaped vision-language interaction, which have demonstrated strong capabilities in visual grounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, reasoning-based segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang, 2025</a>)</cite>, and text-image alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yarom et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, the integration of reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning paradigms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> has significantly expanded the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> have been particularly effective in activating and enhancing the latent logical deduction abilities within these models. These advancements have enabled LLMs to achieve improved performance in complex reasoning tasks, including mathematical reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, fine-grained spatial understanding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and logical reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chollet et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, the introduction of visual chain-of-thought and multi-dimensional perception has significantly enhanced multimodal reasoning in LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">ByteDance, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), allowing them to integrate and reason across both visual and textual modalities. These models’ improved reasoning capabilities have broad implications for real-world applications, including embodied intelligence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shridhar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, game agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and autonomous driving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cui et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, where sophisticated reasoning is required to make complex decisions in dynamic, multimodal environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Against this backdrop, a series of reasoning-oriented multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that inherit advantages from earlier architectural designs have emerged <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Among them, models such as OpenAI 4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hurst et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and Qwen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> have become key reference points for measuring the current level of cross-modal intelligence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Multimodal Reasoning Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Along with the rapid evolution of model capabilities, constructing multidimensional and interpretable evaluation frameworks to systematically characterize the performance of MLLMs across different reasoning levels has become a central challenge in the field <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Early benchmarks, including V*Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie, 2024</a>)</cite>, VisualPuzzles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, VisuLogic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, R-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, and VGRP-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, primarily relied on synthetic tasks to assess abstract reasoning abilities related to logical structure construction and pattern recognition. Subsequently, benchmarks such as MathVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MathVerse <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> further introduced cross-modal mathematical reasoning to examine model performance under scenarios requiring deep integration of symbolic and visual information. Moreover, CityBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and DriveBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> <span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span> further extended evaluation to spatial reasoning in urban scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As an important carrier of high-density geospatial information, map-based visual question answering has gradually evolved into a key research direction for evaluating the depth of multimodal cognition. In this context, MapEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dihan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MapQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, MapIQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and CartoMark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> have systematically revealed, from perspectives ranging from holistic evaluation and basic perception to textual element parsing, the substantial gap between multimodal models and human performance in geospatial cognition, as well as shared limitations in perception-reasoning decoupling and fine-grained semantic understanding.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, at the level of higher-order spatial reasoning, FRIEDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pyo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and GeoX-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> expose structural deficiencies in complex spatial orientation and compositional reasoning, while CartoMapQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ung et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, through hierarchical evaluation in real-world map service scenarios, characterizes reasoning bottlenecks in practical tasks such as scale understanding and route navigation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, although existing benchmarks are able to uncover deficiencies in local perception and specific spatial tasks, their overall coverage of model capabilities remains limited. Most evaluations focus on visual question answering and local perceptual skills, while lacking systematic characterization of global spatial modeling, long-range dependency reasoning, and sequential decision-making. Moreover, existing datasets generally fail to explicitly incorporate multidimensional real-world constraints and user-specific demands, making it difficult to comprehensively reflect the upper bounds of large models’ reasoning and decision-making capabilities in realistic and complex scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Map-Based Spatial Reasoning and Planning</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In multimodal reasoning research, map-based spatial reasoning and planning have become core problems in navigation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Venu and Gurusamy, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ranga et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, intelligent transportation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shoaib et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan and Lv, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen, 2025</a>)</cite>, and autonomous driving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sima et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Compared with traditional perception-driven map understanding tasks, these studies place greater emphasis on a model’s ability to jointly model spatial structures, topological relationships, and long-tracing decision-making.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent works such as CityBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MapLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> explore map-driven spatial reasoning capabilities from different application scenarios, particularly examining model performance in transportation environments and urban contexts. Meanwhile, for embodied navigation tasks, researchers have proposed evaluation frameworks such as PlanAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, PReP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, GeoNav <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and NavBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. These frameworks assess the spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal models from two complementary aspects: navigation understanding and step-by-step execution, thereby promoting a transition from static comprehension to dynamic action generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although several benchmarks have focused on evaluating models’ reasoning and tool-use capabilities in multi-step spatial tasks, for example, GeoBenchX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krechetova and Kochedykov, 2025</a>)</cite>, which examines collaborative reasoning through the integration of multiple geographic functions, and MapBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xing et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which investigates hierarchical reading and attention mechanisms for multi-scale map information from a cognitive science perspective. Other benchmarks such as ReasonMap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>, RewardMap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, and TraveLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> further evaluate autonomous reasoning and decision-making in complex scenarios by incorporating long-tracing logical reasoning, reinforcement learning feedback, and dynamic perturbation settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Nevertheless, despite examining spatial reasoning from multiple dimensions, these benchmarks generally overlook real-world constraints such as time, cost, and comfort, and often rely heavily on external tools, preventing a thorough evaluation of models’ pure visual reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, existing RP-based benchmarks exhibit clear limitations in data scale and task complexity. Most fail to adequately consider multidimensional constraints present in real-world scenarios and struggle to effectively isolate model prior biases. Therefore, there is an urgent need for an evaluation framework that can eliminate prior interference while faithfully reflecting complex constraints and user demands, in order to comprehensively assess the integrated reasoning and decision-making capabilities of MLLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>More Details for Dataset Construction</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>QA Queries Construction</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In MapTab, we design 24 types of QA tasks for both the Metromap and Travelmap scenarios, covering three dimensions: <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Perception-based Reasoning, Local Perception-based Reasoning, and Spatial Relationship Judgment</span>.
The experiments systematically configure four input modalities: <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Map-only, Edge_tab-only, Vertex_tab-only, and Map+Vertex_tab</span>. The introduction of pure tabular modalities (Edge/Vertex-only) fills a gap in existing benchmarks regarding multimodal evaluation with <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">image + structured data</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In particular, for the joint image-table input design in the Metromap scenario, we construct a strict <em id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Cross-modal Necessity</em> setting by removing the <span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Line</span> column. By deliberately eliminating explicit topological cues, we create an <em id="A2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">information gap</em> that forces models to deeply align and fuse visual features from high-resolution maps with semantic information from long-context tables, thereby authentically evaluating multimodal joint reasoning capabilities under single-modality deficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To eliminate instruction bias and enhance evaluation robustness, each QA task category is equipped with five semantically equivalent but stylistically distinct instruction templates. These templates span diverse expression styles, including Direct / Neutral, Simple &amp; Conversational, Slightly Formal, Technical / Academic Style, and Concise / Dataset-Friendly, and are cyclically applied during question generation. Detailed question examples are provided in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 QA Query ‣ Appendix D Query Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 QA Query ‣ Appendix D Query Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>, all QA tasks in this study are strictly limited to binary judgment questions and multiple-choice questions. During answer generation, we adopt a dual-track strategy.
For tasks that can be logically derived from Edge_tab and Vertex_tab, ground-truth answers are automatically generated using Python scripts. For more complex tasks that cannot be fully covered by rule-based logic, the Gemini-3-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2025</a>)</cite> model is invoked for reasoning-based answer generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">During model inference, we apply a structured extraction scheme that precisely captures predictions between two tags <math id="A2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;\text{answer\_begin}&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>answer_begin</mtext><mo>&gt;</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;\text{answer\_begin}&gt;</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;\text{answer\_end}&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>answer_end</mtext><mo>&gt;</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;\text{answer\_end}&gt;</annotation></semantics></math> . To ensure absolute rigor of the benchmark data, all model-generated preliminary answers are subsequently verified and validated through manual inspection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>RP Query Distribution Based on Difficulty Classification Metrics</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To achieve fair and balanced allocation of query numbers for Metromap and Travelmap across training and test sets, we propose the following distribution strategy:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input and target definition:</span>
Given a set of cities/attractions <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>, total query number <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, weighting exponent <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, and minimum query threshold <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>, the algorithm takes these parameters as input and outputs the query number <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> for each city/attraction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Difficulty grouping and target initialization (Phase 1):</span>
Based on the Map Difficulty labels (Hard, Medium, Easy), cities/attractions are divided into three groups <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\text{Easy}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mtext>Easy</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\text{Easy}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\text{Medium}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mtext>Medium</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\text{Medium}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\text{Hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\text{Hard}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The base query number is set as <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{base}=\lfloor Q/3\rfloor" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>base</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{base}=\lfloor Q/3\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math>. The target query numbers for the Medium and Hard groups, <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{Medium}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>Medium</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{Medium}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{Hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>Hard</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{Hard}}</annotation></semantics></math>, are both initialized to this base value, while the remaining queries are assigned to the Easy group as <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{Easy}}=Q-2\times\text{base}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>Easy</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mtext>base</mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{Easy}}=Q-2\times\text{base}</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring conservation of the total query count.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training and test target allocation:</span>
Within each difficulty group, cities/attractions are first separated according to image set type labels (training_set or test_set). Target query numbers <math id="A2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="target_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">target_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="target_{\text{test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">target_{\text{test}}</annotation></semantics></math> are then assigned to ensure a 4:1 ratio between training and test queries.
This ratio applies to query counts rather than image counts (the image ratio is 2:1).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intra-group weighted allocation (Phase 2):</span>
Within each difficulty group and split (six groups in total), intra-group weights are computed based on the <math id="A2.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>-th power of each city’s/attraction’s Vertex Numbers. The total group weight is</p>
<table id="A2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="W=\sum_{c\in S}(c.\text{Vertex Numbers})^{\alpha}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext>Vertex Numbers</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>α</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=\sum_{c\in S}(c.\text{Vertex Numbers})^{\alpha}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.I1.i4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Queries <math id="A2.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> are then allocated proportionally to ensure consistency with these weights.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rounding and minimum threshold constraint:</span>
Within each group, all cities/attractions except the last one apply rounding and enforce the minimum threshold <math id="A2.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The last city/attraction absorbs rounding errors to ensure that the group’s total query count exactly matches <math id="A2.I1.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="target_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">target_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>. This city is recorded as <math id="A2.I1.i5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="LastCity_{d,s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">LastCity_{d,s}</annotation></semantics></math> for later compensation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">6.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Global ratio compensation (Phase 3):</span>
After intra-group allocation, the total number of test queries is checked against the global target of 20% (i.e., <math id="A2.I1.i6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2Q</annotation></semantics></math>).
If an excess <math id="A2.I1.i6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> exists, queries are preferentially deducted from the last city/attraction in the Easy-test group (<math id="A2.I1.i6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="LastCity_{\text{Easy,test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>Easy,test</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">LastCity_{\text{Easy,test}}</annotation></semantics></math>) and evenly compensated to the last cities/attractions in the Medium-training and Hard-training groups (<math id="A2.I1.i6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="LastCity_{d,\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>train</mtext></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">LastCity_{d,\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">7.</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Minimum threshold consistency check:</span>
After compensation, the adjusted last cities/attractions are checked to ensure their query counts do not fall below <math id="A2.I1.i7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If violations occur, the second-to-last city/attraction is introduced into the compensation process, guaranteeing strict enforcement of the minimum threshold while maintaining the 4:1 training-test query ratio.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>

</div>
<div id="alg1.4.1.1.3" class="ltx_listingline">
</div>
<div id="\algocf@printnl@i{{{6}}}alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
                  
                  
                  <span id="\algocf@printnl@i{{{6}}}alg1.l10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each subset type <math id="\algocf@printnl@i{{{6}}}alg1.l10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in\{\text{train, test}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>train, test</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in\{\text{train, test}\}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="\algocf@printnl@i{{{6}}}alg1.l10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
