<section id="A5.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.1.4 </span>Travelmap-Vertex_tab</h4>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on real-world characteristics of tourist attractions and transportation facilities, we design the attributes in the <span id="A5.SS1.SSS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Travelmap Vertex_tab</span> as follows:</p>
<ol id="A5.I4" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A5.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A5.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Time</span>: This attribute is generated as a random integer in the range of 30-180 minutes. For locations such as airports and railway stations, the time is directly set to 0.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.I4.i1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design Rationale</span>: This attribute is intended to simulate the duration of stay at each attraction. Locations such as airports and stations typically do not involve sightseeing activities, and thus their time values are set to 0.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A5.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Price</span>: This attribute is a random integer ranging from 10 to 200 and constrained to be a multiple of 5. For locations such as airports and railway stations, the price is randomly set to 100, 200, or 300.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.I4.i2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design Rationale</span>: This attribute simulates entrance fees for attractions and service costs at transportation hubs. In RP tasks, transportation station costs are counted only at the final destination, while prices at intermediate stations are set to 0, reflecting the cost structures of different attractions and transportation facilities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A5.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comfort Level</span>: This attribute models perceived comfort using a travel-review-style rating scheme. A single-decimal value is randomly generated within the range of 1.0-5.0, with ratings <math id="A5.I4.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> 3.0 accounting for the majority.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.I4.i3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design Rationale</span>: This design simulates tourists’ comfort experiences when visiting attractions or using services at transportation hubs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I4.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A5.I4.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reliability</span>: This attribute is defined as <math id="A5.I4.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a/365" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>365</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a/365</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A5.I4.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> is an integer ranging from 60 to 365, with values greater than 180 occurring more frequently. The final value is reported with six decimal places.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.I4.i4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I4.i4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I4.i4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design Rationale</span>: This attribute simulates the reliability of different attractions or transportation facilities, reflecting whether attractions are open and whether transportation hubs experience service suspensions or closures. Here, <math id="A5.I4.i4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of days per year during which the location is operational; larger values indicate higher reliability.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

id="lstnumberx139.34" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.35" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">that</span><span id="lstnumberx139.36" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.37" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">the</span><span id="lstnumberx139.38" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.39" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">CSV</span><span id="lstnumberx139.40" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.41" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">syntax</span><span id="lstnumberx139.42" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.43" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">between</span><span id="lstnumberx139.44" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.45" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">these</span><span id="lstnumberx139.46" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.47" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">two</span><span id="lstnumberx139.48" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.49" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">tags</span><span id="lstnumberx139.50" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.51" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">is</span><span id="lstnumberx139.52" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.53" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">absolutely</span><span id="lstnumberx139.54" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx139.55" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">correct</span>.
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Prompts for RP Queries</h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For RP tasks, the prompts in the Metromap dataset are divided into a total of 12 categories. Among them, three categories correspond to unconstrained prompts under different input modalities, namely Map-only, Edge_tab-only, and Map+Edge_tab. The remaining nine categories involve prompts with single or multiple constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, in constrained Metromap scenarios, in order to enable a comprehensive consideration of different evaluation dimensions, normalization or transformation operations are applied to the indicators Time, Price, Comfort Level, Reliability, and Transfer Time. The specific preprocessing rules are as follows:</p>
<ol id="A5.I5" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A5.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A5.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I5.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Time</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I5.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,3]</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly scaled to <math id="A5.I5.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A5.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I5.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Price</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I5.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1.5]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1.5]</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly scaled to <math id="A5.I5.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I5.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A5.I5.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I5.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I5.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transfer Time</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I5.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[5,15]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[5,15]</annotation></semantics></math> is scaled according to the same benchmark ratio as <math id="A5.I5.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,3]</annotation></semantics></math>, so as to ensure that transfer behaviors are assigned a significant penalty weight.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I5.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A5.I5.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I5.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I5.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comfort Level and Reliability</span>: Comfort and reliability (originally in the range <math id="A5.I5.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>) are subjected to an inverse transformation (i.e., <math id="A5.I5.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-x</annotation></semantics></math>) when jointly considered with other factors, and zero values are removed.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Similarly, for constrained Travelmap datasets, the four indicators, Time, Price, Comfort Level, and Reliability, also require corresponding scaling or inversion operations. The specific rules are as follows:</p>
<ol id="A5.I6" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A5.I6.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A5.I6.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I6.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I6.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Time</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I6.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,180]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,180</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,180]</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly scaled to <math id="A5.I6.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. If the range is larger, scaling is still performed based on the <math id="A5.I6.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,180]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,180</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,180]</annotation></semantics></math> interval.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I6.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A5.I6.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I6.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I6.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Price</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I6.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,200]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,200</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,200]</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly scaled to <math id="A5.I6.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. If the range is larger, scaling is still performed based on the <math id="A5.I6.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,200]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,200</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,200]</annotation></semantics></math> interval.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I6.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A5.I6.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I6.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I6.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comfort Level</span>: The original value range <math id="A5.I6.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,5]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,5]</annotation></semantics></math> is linearly scaled to <math id="A5.I6.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I6.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A5.I6.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I6.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I6.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comfort Level and Reliability</span>: Comfort and reliability (in the range <math id="A5.I6.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>) are subjected to an inverse transformation (i.e., <math id="A5.I6.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-x</annotation></semantics></math>) when jointly considered with other factors, and zero values are removed.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, to construct <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex2_tab</span>, we integrate part of the information from <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edge_tab</span> into <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex_tab</span>. The merging strategy is as follows: in Metromap, the <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Price</span> column of <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex2_tab</span> is computed as the mean price of all edges associated with the corresponding node in <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Edge_tab</span>, while the remaining attributes remain identical to those in the original <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex_tab</span>. In Travelmap, all attribute values from the original <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertex_tab</span> are directly retained without any integration.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the following, we only elaborate on the prompts adopted by the five experimental configurations listed in Table <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS1" title="4.2.1 Performance of MLLMs on RP ‣ 4.2 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<div id="A5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>

<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Prompts for QA Queries</h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the QA tasks, a total of 24 questions are designed across the Metromap and Travelmap scenarios. In Metromap, four input modalities: <span id="A5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Map-Only, Edge_Tab-Only, Vertex_Tab-Only, and Map + Vertex Tab</span> are considered, covering three categories of problems: Global Perception-based Reasoning tasks (GP), Local Perception-based Reasoning tasks (LP), and Spatial Relationship Judgment tasks (SR). This paper reports only the prompts corresponding to the Map + Vertex_Tab input setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<div id="A5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>
<div id="lstnumberx317" class="ltx_listingline">#<span id="lstnumberx317.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx317.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">Role</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx318" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx318.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">You</span><span id="lstnumberx318.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx318.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">are</span><span id="lstnumberx318.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx318.5" class="ltx_text <section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>More Experiments</h2>

<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Experimental Settings</h3>

<section id="A6.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">F.1.1 </span>Model Selection Criteria</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model selection is guided by evaluation requirements centered on the RP task, and two filtering criteria are applied accordingly:</p>
<ol id="A6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Models that cannot meet long-context requirements are excluded (e.g., DeepSeek-VL2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), as the input length of some samples exceeds 32k tokens.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Models that support long-context inputs but tend to exhibit reasoning loops or excessive deliberation in complex RP tasks, resulting in unstable or poorly structured outputs, are also excluded, such as llava-v1.6-mistral-hf (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, Ovis2.5 (9B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, and Glyph (10B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">F.1.2 </span>Model Parameter Settings</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Open-source models are primarily evaluated using the vLLM inference framework on a cluster equipped with four NVIDIA A100 GPUs. To ensure reproducibility, all experiments uniformly set <span id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">temperature</span> to 0.0, <span id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">maximum_generation_length</span> to 2,048 tokens, and extend <span id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">max_model_len</span> to the maximum supported by each model. Some open-source models are accessed via third-party APIs, with other parameters kept at official default settings; closed-source models are evaluated through their official APIs, following the default configurations specified in the corresponding technical documentation. For models equipped with a Thinking mechanism, the <span id="A6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">thinking_budget</span> is uniformly set to 4,096 tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">F.1.3 </span>Input Preprocessing</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tabular data are primarily provided in CSV format, with a small number of samples using JSON format. Visual inputs adopt an adaptive preprocessing strategy: for models that support arbitrary resolutions, original images are preserved; when image dimensions exceed model limits, images are resized to the maximum allowable size while maintaining the original aspect ratio; for models that enforce a fixed aspect ratio (e.g., square inputs), non-uniform stretching is applied. Although this operation alters the geometric proportions of the images, it preserves key topological structures and textual forms, thereby ensuring the readability of semantic information.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="A6.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A6.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Atomic Capability Distribution and Performance Bottleneck Analysis in Multimodal QA Tasks</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically characterize the capability structure and performance bottlenecks of models in multimodal QA tasks, we first categorize all questions by task type and further summarize the underlying atomic capabilities they rely on. As shown in Table <a href="#A6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, in both the Metromap and Travelmap scenarios, question difficulty is graded based on the overall performance of different models: questions that almost all models fail to answer correctly are defined as <span id="A6.I2.i1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hard</span>, questions with significant performance variance across models are categorized as <span id="A6.I2.i1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Medium</span>, and questions on which most models perform well are labeled as <span id="A6.I2.i1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Easy</span>. On this basis, we systematically summarize the core atomic capabilities involved in questions of different difficulty levels by jointly considering question semantics and solution procedures.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Experimental results show that the primary performance bottlenecks in multimodal QA tasks are concentrated in <span id="A6.I2.i1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">numerical reasoning ability and native intuitive visual reasoning ability</span>. In contrast, for perceptual tasks such as target localization and retrieval in images and tables, model performance is relatively stable and mature. A clear performance divergence is observed across different types of perceptual and reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, the majority of questions involving counting, numerical comparison, and numerical computation, as well as tasks relying on native intuitive visual reasoning (e.g., path trajectory tracing and trajectory intersection detection), are mainly distributed in the <span id="A6.I2.i1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hard</span> and <span id="A6.I2.i1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Medium</span> difficulty ranges. This result indicates that, in complex QA scenarios, the key bottlenecks of current open-source multimodal models still lie in the insufficient ability to precisely model numerical relationships and the lack of high-level visual intuitive reasoning. In contrast, nearly all questions focused on localization capabilities, whether in image-based tasks that require identifying target elements within images or in table-based tasks that require retrieving corresponding entries from structured tables, and are categorized as <span id="A6.I2.i1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Easy</span>, reflecting that localization, as a lower-level perceptual skill, has become a widely available and stable strength of existing models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Further analysis based on Table D2 shows that the most challenging tasks are concentrated in three representative questions: (1) the <span id="A6.I2.i1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M+V-GP</span> question in the Metromap scenario: “What is the total stop time of the subway line with the longest stop time?”; (2) the <span id="A6.I2.i1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M-GP</span> question in the Travelmap scenario: “How many tourist attractions are there in total?”; and (3) the <span id="A6.I2.i1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M+V-SR</span> question in the Travelmap scenario: “What is the cost of the lowest-priced location adjacent to {Spot A}?”</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, the experimental results clearly demonstrate that the core performance bottleneck of current multimodal models in complex QA scenarios lies in their limited <span id="A6.I2.i1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">multi-hop reasoning capability</span>. Although these questions differ substantially in their surface forms, they share a common structural requirement at the capability level: all of them require models to perform <span id="A6.I2.i1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text">cross-modal, multi-step sequential reasoning</span> grounded in complex visual or structured inputs. Unlike tasks that rely on single-step judgments, such problems demand consistent information propagation and integration across multiple intermediate reasoning states. During multi-step reasoning, perceptual errors, relational modeling biases, or numerical instabilities introduced at early stages tend to accumulate and be progressively amplified in subsequent steps, ultimately leading to systemic failure of the entire reasoning chain. Consequently, <span id="A6.I2.i1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the key challenge of multimodal QA does not stem from the deficiency of any individual module, but rather from a structural performance ceiling dominated by error accumulation throughout the multi-hop reasoning process</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A6.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mechanism Analysis of Explicit Chain-of-Thought in Multimodal QA Tasks</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results in Table <a href="#A6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> show that introducing Explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) significantly improves overall reasoning performance in multimodal QA tasks, but does not substantially enhance perceptual capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, explicit CoT fails to yield noticeable gains in the following task types:
(1) <span id="A6.I2.i2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M-GP</span> in Metromap (Visual perception, Counting);
(2) <span id="A6.I2.i2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M-SR</span> in Metromap (Target localization);
(3) <span id="A6.I2.i2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M+V-LP</span> in Travelmap (Graph trajectory tracing, Target localization, Numerical computation);
(4) <span id="A6.I2.i2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M+V-SR</span> in Travelmap (Target localization, Numerical comparison).</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These tasks are primarily limited by insufficient perception and structural understanding at the image or chart level. As perceptual errors accumulate across reasoning steps, explicit CoT cannot effectively translate enhanced intermediate reasoning into final performance gains. This demonstrates that <span id="A6.I2.i2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CoT is only effective when reliable perception has already been established, and cannot compensate for perceptual deficiencies</span>. Therefore, in complex multimodal QA scenarios, perceptual bottlenecks directly cap the upper bound of performance gains achievable through structured guidance at the reasoning stage.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A6.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Perception-Domain Ablation Analysis</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#A6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ F.2 Performance of MLLMs on QA ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, perception-domain ablation reveals significant differences in how perceptual capabilities affect multimodal QA performance, with <span id="A6.I2.i3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">global perception-related tasks constituting the primary bottleneck</span>. Global Perception-based Reasoning (GP) tasks are heavily concentrated in the <span id="A6.I2.i3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hard</span> category (5 Hard, 1 Easy), significantly exceeding Local Perception-based Reasoning (LP) and Spatial Relationship (SR) tasks, which exhibit either Easy-dominant or balanced distributions.This result indicates that models have already developed relatively stable capabilities for local target localization and local perceptual reasoning; however, once the perceptual scope expands to a global scale, their performance degrades markedly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From a mechanistic perspective, the high difficulty of global perception tasks primarily stems from their broader perceptual scope and higher structural complexity. Unlike local perception tasks, which require attention to a limited region or a single object, global tasks demand that models integrate multiple dispersed targets and their structural relationships across wide-ranging visual inputs, thereby imposing substantially greater requirements on attention allocation and information fusion. Moreover, global scenes often contain a large amount of irrelevant and distracting information, requiring models to suppress noise while maintaining sustained focus on critical regions. This substantially increases the risk that perceptual errors accumulate during multi-step reasoning, which may ultimately lead to the failure of the entire reasoning process.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.I2.i3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I2.i3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, the perceptual-domain ablation analysis reveals the systemic difficulty of global perception tasks and their limiting effect on multimodal QA performance. While models have become relatively mature in local perceptual capabilities, they still exhibit pronounced bottlenecks in large-scale information integration and interference suppression. This finding provides clear guidance for future model improvements, highlighting the importance of enhancing perceptual structural modeling and the robustness of multi-hop reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A6.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="A6.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Difficulty statistics of different questions in the Metromap and Travelmap scenarios. Questions that models almost entirely fail to answer are categorized as “Hard”; questions with substantial performance variance across models are categorized as “Medium”; and questions on which models generally perform well are categorized as “Easy”. Each question is further classified by the underlying capabilities it requires, enabling an analysis of which abilities models still have room to improve.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Ablation study of Map difficulty and Query difficulty</h3>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A6.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ F.3 Ablation study of Map difficulty and Query difficulty ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates in detail the distribution of model accuracy across different input modalities as a function of Map Difficulty and Query Difficulty. We observed distinctly different performance decay patterns between the two datasets:</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A6.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A6.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A6.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Polarized Performance and Reasoning Collapse in Metromap:</span> In the Metromap scenario, the accuracy distribution exhibits significant <span id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">imbalance</span>. Models perform reasonably well on “Easy" samples, but experience a <span id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">precipitous drop</span> on "Medium" and "Hard" levels, with accuracy for “Hard" samples approaching zero. This phenomenon indicates that the high-level topological structures in Metromap, such as complex transfer networks and densely connected nodes, have reached or even exceeded the <span id="A6.I3.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cognitive capacity ceiling</span> of current models. Once the graph complexity surpasses a critical threshold, the reasoning ability collapses systematically rather than declining gradually.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A6.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear Decay and Adaptivity in Travelmap:</span> In contrast, Travelmap shows a more stable performance across difficulty levels, exhibiting a uniform distribution. Although accuracy decreases with increasing difficulty, the decay curve remains gradual without functional failure. This suggests that the topological logic in Travelmap, even in the Hard mode, largely remains within the models’ effective reasoning boundary, allowing them to maintain relatively stable generalization capabilities.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

and M+V2 denotes Map + Vertex2_tab.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Through a cross-analysis of Map Difficulty and Query Difficulty, Figure <a href="#A6.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ F.3 Ablation study of Map difficulty and Query difficulty ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents a more fine-grained distribution of performance gradients. Overall, model accuracy exhibits a pronounced stepwise decline as task complexity increases, progressively degrading from the Easy-Easy combination to the Hard-Hard combination.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Further fine-grained analysis reveals clear differences in sensitivity to the sources of complexity across task scenarios. In the Metromap task, map topological complexity has a significantly greater impact on final performance than query logical complexity, indicating that the overall visual complexity and information density of metro network diagrams constitute the primary challenge. In contrast, in the Travelmap task, query logical complexity exerts a substantially stronger influence on performance than map topological complexity, suggesting that the reasoning structure of the queries and multi-step logical composition are the key limiting factors in this scenario.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These results demonstrate that the dominant factors constraining model performance vary across task scenarios. Consequently, distinct optimization strategies are required for scenarios dominated by perceptual complexity versus those dominated by reasoning complexity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Ablation study of QA for resolution</h3>

<figure id="A6.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F6.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="A6.F6.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Metromap Scenario</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A6.F6.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18600v1/Figures/res_travelmap_qa.png" id="A6.F6.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/271;" width="476" height="271" alt="Refer to caption">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A6.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Effects of different image resolutions on QA task performance in the Metromap (a) and Travelmap (b) scenarios. Images are proportionally downsampled to <math id="A6.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A6.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A6.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A6.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/16</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A6.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/32</annotation></semantics></math> of the original resolution. Evaluation is conducted under six Map-based input settings: Map-GP (M-GP), Map-LP (M-LP), Map-SR (M-SR), Map+Vertex_tab-GP (M+V-GP), Map+Vertex_tab-LP (M+V-LP), and Map+Vertex_tab-SR (M+V-SR).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For QA queries, experimental results indicate that improvements in image clarity are not a sufficient condition for enhancing model performance. On the contrary, for multiple categories of questions, moderately downsampled images often lead to better reasoning outcomes. In some tasks, model accuracy even exhibits a stable upward trend as the degree of downsampling increases. This phenomenon suggests that the sampling rate itself is not the key determinant of model performance. Instead, model behavior is more strongly constrained by the perceptual granularity and reasoning paradigm required by the specific task. When a task primarily relies on global structural understanding or high-level semantic abstraction, reducing visual redundancy can help suppress irrelevant details, thereby enabling the model to focus more effectively on information that is critical for reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.5 </span>Ablation study of Tabular Modality</h3>

<div id="A6.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Setup.</span>
We adopt two table formats, namely CSV and JSON, for the tabular modality. Table <a href="#A6.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ F.5 Ablation study of Tabular Modality ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reports the token counts of three table types, including Edge_tab, Vertex_tab, and Vertex2_tab, under both formats. In addition, Table <a href="#A6.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ F.5 Ablation study of Tabular Modality ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> investigates the performance of CSV and JSON formats in two constraint-aware RP settings, namely Map+Edge_tab+Vertex_tab and Map+Vertex2_tab, analyzing whether different table representations affect the model’s perception and understanding of tabular content. Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ F.5 Ablation study of Tabular Modality ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> further presents comparative experimental results of the two formats on QA queries.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Results.</span>
We initially hypothesized that the JSON format would provide stronger structural cues and thus improve model understanding and overall performance, whereas the CSV format, despite being more token-efficient, might suffer from weaker interpretability. However, experimental results reveal that although the CSV format uses more than 50% fewer tokens than the JSON format, its performance is not inferior in either RP or QA tasks, and even outperforms JSON in certain cases. This indicates that while the JSON format offers richer structural information, it does not increase the upper bound of model perception and reasoning capabilities. On the contrary, the longer context induced by JSON representations may sometimes hinder reasoning performance.</p>
</div>

<section id="A6.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.6 </span>Ablation study of Language</h3>

<div id="A6.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A6.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> presents the overall language distribution in the Metromap and Travelmap scenarios using a mixed statistical approach, retaining only the top five categories by proportion and aggregating the remaining categories. Figure <a href="#A6.F7.sf1" title="Figure 7(a) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(a)</span></a> shows the distribution of the native language of the locations corresponding to the images, covering a total of 328 images. The results indicate that locations with Chinese as the native language account for the highest proportion at 52.1%, followed by English at 24.4%. Figure <a href="#A6.F7.sf2" title="Figure 7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(b)</span></a> further summarizes the actual language used in the images, also based on 328 images, showing a distribution trend similar to that of the native language statistics, with Chinese being the most frequently used and English second. Based on these observations, Figure <a href="#A6.F7.sf3" title="Figure 7(c) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(c)</span></a> categorizes the languages into Chinese, English, and Others, denoted as Chinese, English, and Others, respectively, and further divides them into nine combinations according to the mother_tongue-image_language pairing. Since the combinations Chinese-English, Chinese-Others, and English-Chinese do not appear in the data, the analysis focuses on the remaining six categories. The results show that the Chinese-Chinese combination has the highest proportion at 58.4%.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Experimental results in Table <a href="#A6.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ F.6 Ablation study of Language ‣ Appendix F More Experiments ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> indicate a significant language bias in model performance: across regional datasets, when the input uses a dominant language (Chinese or English), the model consistently performs better than in cases using other languages. This phenomenon is highly correlated with the frequency distribution of different languages in the training corpus, reflecting the model’s stronger adaptation to high-frequency languages. Meanwhile, the model does not exhibit a significant language prior based on geographic or regional knowledge. When the native language of the location corresponding to the image does not match the language actually used in the data, model performance does not show systematic variation, indicating that the key factor affecting model performance is the language used in the sample itself rather than the native language attribute of the location.</p>
</div>

<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Error Case Analysis</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the experimental results, after excluding anomalies caused by repeated generation or answer collapse in certain small-scale open-source models  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we randomly sampled and analyzed 100 erroneous predictions from the entire set of errors, with 50 from models with explicit reasoning mechanisms and 50 from models without. Systematic analysis indicates that these errors mainly reflect three key deficiencies in current vision-language models: shortcomings in instruction-following ability, insufficient symbolic visual perception, and imbalanced reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First</span>, some small-scale open-source vision-language models exhibit significant issues in following instructions in complex scenarios. Our chart-modality collaborative multi-constraint RP tasks involve high input complexity, consisting of a map image, two structured tables, and multiple fine-grained, interrelated constraints (as described in <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Prompts for RP Queries ‣ Appendix E Prompt Template ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>), including explicit definitions of start and end points, fixed output formats, and multi-factor weighting. For small-scale open-source models (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B), the overall ability to follow multiple complex instructions under long-context conditions remains limited, especially when it comes to consistently adhering to key constraints that are concise yet critical for correctness. Specifically, Qwen3-VL-8B in some samples even misinterpreted the basic definitions of start and end points (see Figure <a href="#A7.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>); in other samples, although the model successfully inferred the correct path, it failed to comply with the instruction to annotate “(transfer)” after transfer stations, leading to outputs being judged as incorrect (see Figure <a href="#A7.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Second</span>, even highly capable vision models continue to encounter challenges in fine-grained symbolic reasoning. Unlike object-centric natural images, the subway and tourist maps we use are essentially highly structured graphical visual representations, with core information encoded as topological relationships and symbolic logic. Natural images typically exhibit “sparse information, dense features," e.g., a rectangular region containing a cat has many contiguous pixel features supporting the recognition of object class, appearance, and texture. In contrast, subway and tourist maps often have large blank backgrounds and sparse low-level visual features, yet extremely high information density: a single area may contain multiple overlapping lines of different colors, with intersections overlaid with transfer station names and adjacent line labels. Therefore, these tasks require the model to possess near-human symbolic visual perception, i.e., to accurately parse and track visual information in complex stacking and irregular layouts with symbols as the focus. However, error analysis shows that this ability remains generally insufficient in current models. Even high-performance closed-source models such as Gemini-3-Flash sometimes fail to consistently and accurately track continuous subway line trajectories (see Figure <a href="#A7.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>); in areas with dense multiple lines, the model may exhibit “line-jumping,” i.e., jumping unrealistically from one line’s station to another’s (see Figure <a href="#A7.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Finally</span>, vision-language models exhibit a dual imbalance in reasoning: “overthinking simple problems and underthinking complex problems.” After excluding perception factors, error analysis further revealed two typical reasoning issues. On the one hand, some models with explicit reasoning mechanisms tend to overthink relatively simple tasks, leading to performance degradation. As shown in Figure <a href="#A7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, for a problem with Map_Difficulty = Easy, Query_Difficulty = Medium, and Difficulty_score = 3, Qwen3-VL-Plus can directly produce the correct answer without the reasoning mechanism enabled; however, enabling the reasoning mechanism results in errors. Detailed analysis of its reasoning process shows that the model performed up to 25 <span id="A7.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wait</span> operations, frequently doubting, self-correcting, and switching thought paths, which not only reduced reasoning efficiency but also truncated the reasoning process and interfered with an originally correct solution. On the other hand, for reasoning problems requiring explicit comparison of multiple attributes and constraint optimization, the current models’ computation and reasoning capabilities are still insufficient. As shown in Figure <a href="#A7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix G Error Case Analysis ‣ MapTab: Can MLLMs Master Constrained Route Planning?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, even with only two candidate paths, Gemini-3-Flash failed to accurately calculate and compare the relevant attribute values to select the optimal path satisfying the constraints, instead resorting to approximate guessing based on the shortest path.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18600v1/error_case/case_1.png" id="A7.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/296;" width="381" height="296" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A7.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A7.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Error Case 1: Wrong source and destination</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18600v1/error_case/case_2.png" id="A7.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/298;" width="381" height="298" alt="Refer to caption">

<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite providing a high-quality multimodal benchmark, this study has several limitations:</p>
<ol id="A8.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A8.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A8.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Limited Map Diversity.</span> The current evaluation is limited to topological graph scenarios, such as metro and attraction maps. In principle, more complex cartographic representations, including large-scale urban maps or remote sensing maps, could also be transformed into heterogeneous graphs for systematic assessment. Extending MapTab to these richer map types would enhance the generality and applicability of the framework.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A8.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A8.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Lack of Dynamic Evaluation.</span> This study primarily relies on static maps and predefined constraints, without incorporating dynamic environments or real-time information updates. Future research should examine model performance under temporally evolving conditions, where constraints and graph structures may change in real time, to better simulate realistic decision-making scenarios.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A8.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A8.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Deficiencies in Model Reasoning.</span> Experimental results indicate that current MLLMs still exhibit notable deficiencies in complex visual perception, multi-dimensional constraint parsing, and long-tracing numerical or compositional reasoning. These findings highlight the need for future model development to prioritize improvements in these core capabilities, thereby enhancing robustness, generalization, and overall reasoning performance in multimodal, multi-constraint tasks.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
